title: Senior Living Research Digest — New This Week — 2026-09-28
secondary_audience: families, caregivers, and senior living professionals

studies.title: Nine years of cycling later: these older athletes still outperform 99% of their peers — even as aging took its toll
studies.the_study: Researchers at King's College London re-tested 82 of 125 lifelong recreational cyclists (53 men, 29 women) nine years after an initial assessment, when participants were 64 to 86 years old. Peak oxygen consumption fell by 19.7%, lean tissue dropped 8.1%, and body fat rose from 23.8% to 29.2%, while blood pressure and metabolic markers stayed in normal ranges. Despite the declines, 98.7% of those completing the fitness test still scored at or above the 90th percentile compared with general reference populations. Cyclists who developed poorly controlled disease (mostly cardiovascular) lost aerobic capacity faster than the disease-free group (24.2% vs 17.3%), but nearly every other measure was similar across health categories.
studies.why_it_matters: It is one of the few long-term studies to follow highly active older adults across nearly a decade, showing that sustained exercise does not stop aging but keeps function far above typical levels — even after illness appears.
studies.story_angle_primary: Aging will still chip away at your aerobic capacity and muscle no matter how much you ride, but this study suggests staying active keeps you functioning at a level most people decades younger never reach — and that the benefit holds even if you develop a manageable chronic condition. If you already exercise, the message is to keep going rather than stopping after a diagnosis; if you don't, talk to your doctor about where to start safely.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For senior living activity directors and caregivers: the finding that lean mass dropped 8% and body fat rose even in dedicated endurance athletes is a reminder that aerobic exercise alone does not protect muscle — resistance and strength programming deserves equal billing in wellness calendars.
studies.caveats: Observational with no control group and substantial attrition (82 of 125 returned); the authors themselves flag survivor bias; participants are unusually fit volunteers who do not represent typical older adults; single research center.

studies.title: New Alzheimer's drugs slow decline — but a pooled analysis says the benefit may be too small for patients to notice
studies.the_study: Neurologists pooled seven randomized placebo-controlled trials of the three anti-amyloid antibodies — aducanumab, lecanemab and donanemab — in people with early symptomatic Alzheimer's disease. All three produced statistically significant but small improvements on cognitive and functional scales (CDR-SB difference of 0.41 points; MMSE 0.44 points). Meanwhile, brain swelling (ARIA-E) occurred in 23.9% of treated participants versus 1.9% on placebo, and microbleeds (ARIA-H) in 16.8% versus 6.8%. APOE ε4 carriers had more than double the swelling risk of non-carriers (29.3% vs 13.8%).
studies.why_it_matters: These are the first disease-modifying Alzheimer's drugs to reach the market, and this synthesis puts hard numbers on the trade-off families are being asked to weigh in the clinic.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you or a family member are considering lecanemab or donanemab, this analysis gives you concrete questions to bring to the appointment: how much slowing should I realistically expect, what will the MRI monitoring schedule involve, and have I had APOE genetic testing — because carrying the ε4 variant roughly doubles the risk of treatment-related brain swelling.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For care partners and senior living clinical staff: infusion schedules and repeated MRI surveillance are a real logistical and transport burden, and knowing that one in four treated patients develops ARIA means having a plan for recognizing new headaches, confusion or visual changes.
studies.caveats: Meta-analysis of trials largely funded by drug manufacturers; brain-volume loss, ventricular enlargement and treatment-related deaths were described narratively but not statistically pooled; trials enrolled early-stage patients, so results may not apply to more advanced dementia; short follow-up relative to a decades-long disease.

studies.title: Across 1.2 million people, lithium users had about 37% less dementia — but no one has proven the drug is the reason
studies.the_study: Italian researchers systematically reviewed 23 studies covering more than 1.2 million people examining whether lithium exposure — from psychiatric prescriptions or naturally occurring levels in drinking water — relates to dementia risk. Pooling four cohort studies produced a hazard ratio of 0.633, roughly a 37% lower risk of dementia among those exposed. Three small randomized trials of cognitive outcomes (229 participants total) also favored lithium, and two ecological studies of water lithium levels pointed the same direction.
studies.why_it_matters: Lithium is an inexpensive, decades-old drug, and consistent signals of this size make it one of the more credible repurposing candidates in dementia prevention — though the evidence remains far short of a recommendation.
studies.story_angle_primary: This is a reason for curiosity, not a reason to ask for a prescription: lithium carries real risks to kidneys and thyroid, requires blood monitoring, and no trial has yet shown it prevents dementia. If you already take lithium for a mood disorder, this is reassuring context rather than a signal to change anything — and never take lithium supplements based on headlines.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For clinicians and care staff: expect questions from residents and families who see coverage of this. The useful framing is that large, long-term randomized trials are still needed, and observational associations of this kind have repeatedly failed to hold up when tested.
studies.caveats: Predominantly observational evidence that cannot establish causation; substantial heterogeneity between studies; randomized data limited to just 229 participants with cognitive (not dementia incidence) outcomes; ecological studies of water lithium cannot account for individual exposure; possible confounding by indication among psychiatric patients.

studies.title: Virtual reality "positive psychology" sessions eased stress for older Korean immigrants who faced discrimination
studies.the_study: Researchers randomized 31 Korean immigrants aged 60 and older (mean age 80.9, two-thirds women, in the U.S. an average of nearly 40 years) who had experienced discrimination during the COVID-19 pandemic to either a three-week, four-module virtual reality program built around noticing, amplifying and practicing positive events, or a wait-list control group. After adjusting for demographics, the VR group reported significantly larger drops in discrimination-related stress and general perceived stress, plus greater gains in life engagement. The program was culturally tailored in both language and content, and older participants completed it.
studies.why_it_matters: It is one of the first trials to show that adults in their 80s will readily use a VR headset and that a short, culturally tailored mental health program can measurably reduce stress tied to discrimination — a source of distress rarely addressed in standard senior services.
studies.story_angle_primary: If stress from unfair or hostile treatment weighs on you, know that brief structured practices focused on noticing and savoring good moments are being tested with people your age — and that being 80-plus is no barrier to using a VR headset. Ask your senior center or community organization whether they offer well-being programs in your language and cultural context.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For activity directors and community program planners: this is early evidence that immersive technology plus cultural tailoring — not one without the other — is what made the program land. It also signals that discrimination-related stress is a legitimate, addressable target in programming for immigrant elders.
studies.caveats: Very small sample (N=31, single site), wait-list control means participants knew their assignment, all outcomes self-reported, three-week program with no long-term follow-up, and findings may not generalize beyond older Korean immigrants.

studies.title: Ambroxol for Parkinson's and Gaucher disease: the hype is running ahead of the evidence
studies.the_study: Researchers systematically reviewed all clinical evidence on ambroxol — a cough medicine repurposed as a possible brain-penetrating treatment for Gaucher disease and GBA1-related Parkinson's disease — screening 137 records and including 20 clinical outcome reports. Evidence in Gaucher disease came mainly from small, uncontrolled and sometimes overlapping case series with inconsistent outcome definitions. For GBA1-related Parkinson's, the key AMBITIOUS trial exists only as a non-peer-reviewed preprint and did not show disease modification; safety data on long-term high-dose use remain limited.
studies.why_it_matters: Ambroxol has been widely discussed in Parkinson's patient communities as a promising disease-modifying option, and this review makes clear it remains off-label and investigational, with biomarker improvements that have not translated into proven clinical benefit.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you have Parkinson's disease with a GBA1 mutation and have read that ambroxol may slow it down, bring this review to your neurologist before buying it or increasing a dose: as of now, improved lab markers have not been shown to mean better symptoms or slower decline, and the safety of long-term high doses is not established.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For families and care staff: patients may be self-sourcing ambroxol based on online enthusiasm. Ask what supplements and off-label medications are actually in the pill organizer, and make sure the prescribing clinician knows.
studies.caveats: Systematic review of heterogeneous, mostly small and uncontrolled studies; meta-analysis was not possible; a pivotal trial is available only as a preprint; all three authors were investigators on one of the included cohort reports (disclosed).

studies.title: Twelve weeks of strength training didn't change older men's appetite one way or the other
studies.the_study: In a secondary analysis of a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 33 older men (average age 67, average BMI 25.4) either did supervised resistance exercise twice a week at 80% of their one-repetition maximum or continued their usual activity for 12 weeks. Appetite — hunger, fullness, satiety and how much food they expected to eat — was tracked across a full 24 hours inside a metabolic chamber before and after. There were no significant differences between the groups on any appetite measure.
studies.why_it_matters: Appetite loss and unintentional weight loss are serious risks in later life, and some older adults avoid strength training for fear of throwing off their eating; this trial suggests resistance training neither suppresses nor stokes appetite in older men.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you have been hesitant to start strength training because you worry it will leave you ravenous or, conversely, put you off your food, this trial found neither happened over three months — so appetite concerns are not a good reason to skip resistance work and its proven benefits for strength, balance and mood.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For dietitians and fitness staff in senior living: introducing a twice-weekly resistance program appears unlikely to disrupt residents' eating patterns, but it also won't be a tool for stimulating appetite in residents who are undereating.
studies.caveats: Small sample (N=33), men only, secondary pooled analysis of a trial not designed for this question, generally healthy normal-weight participants who may not represent frail or underweight elders, self-reported appetite ratings, 12-week duration, single research unit.

studies.title: Staying active still protects thinking skills in your 80s and 90s, 30-year Jerusalem study finds
studies.the_study: Researchers followed a community-dwelling cohort born in 1920-1921 in Jerusalem from 1990 to 2023, assessing participants at ages 70, 78, 85, 90, 95 and 100 (n = 604, 1,024, 1,222, 729, 508 and 205 at each age). Physical activity was self-reported and split into sedentary (under 4 hours a week) versus active (more than 4 hours a week), and cognitive impairment was defined as an MMSE score of 23 or below. Being sedentary at age 78 roughly tripled the odds of cognitive impairment by 85 (OR 2.90), and being sedentary at 70 more than doubled the odds by 78 (OR 2.61); a similar but non-significant pattern appeared between 90 and 95. The share of people who were active dropped sharply after 85, from 64% to 16%.
studies.why_it_matters: Most evidence on exercise and brain health comes from people in their 60s and 70s; this extends it into the ninth and tenth decades, suggesting there is no age at which movement stops mattering for cognition.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you are in your late 70s or 80s, the four-hour-a-week threshold used in this study is modest — roughly 35 minutes a day of walking, gardening or classes. The steep drop-off in activity after 85 in this cohort suggests many people quit earlier than they need to; it is worth asking your clinician what level of activity is safe for you rather than assuming activity is behind you.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For senior living operators, the collapse in activity rates between ages 85 and 90 is a programming signal: exercise offerings often assume an independent-living resident, leaving the oldest and frailest residents with little on the calendar that counts as real movement.
studies.caveats: Observational design — cannot prove exercise causes better cognition, and early cognitive decline may itself reduce activity (reverse causation). Physical activity was self-reported, cognition was screened with the MMSE alone, and the cohort is a single birth cohort from Jerusalem, which may not generalize.

studies.title: Only about 1 in 9 memory clinic patients qualified for the new Alzheimer's drug
studies.the_study: An Italian memory clinic retrospectively reviewed 179 consecutive patients with new-onset cognitive symptoms (mean age 72.3, mean MMSE 26.4) seen between October 2024 and March 2026, testing amyloid status by spinal fluid or PET scan. Alzheimer's disease was diagnosed clinically in 44%, but only 26% were amyloid-positive, and just 21 patients — 11.7% of everyone assessed, and 45.6% of those who were amyloid-positive — met all appropriate-use criteria for the anti-amyloid drug donanemab. Adding a requirement for spinal-fluid p-tau positivity cut eligibility to 13 patients, or 7.3%.
studies.why_it_matters: Families hearing about "breakthrough" Alzheimer's drugs need realistic expectations: in a real clinic, most people with memory complaints — including many diagnosed with Alzheimer's — do not qualify, often because they lack amyloid or have risk factors that make treatment unsafe.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you or your spouse has been told about amyloid-lowering drugs, ask specifically what confirms the diagnosis — a clinical impression is not enough, and this study found that clinical Alzheimer's diagnoses and amyloid test results disagreed often. Ask which eligibility criteria you meet and which you do not, and what the plan is if you are not a candidate.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For care professionals fielding questions about new drugs, this gives a concrete counseling number: expect roughly one in ten people coming through the door to be eligible, and prepare families for the possibility that biomarker testing will redirect the diagnosis entirely.
studies.caveats: Single-center, retrospective, and Italian — referral patterns and diagnostic access differ by country. Relatively small sample (n = 179), and eligibility was estimated on paper rather than tracked through actual treatment decisions or outcomes.

studies.title: Frail stroke patients are far less likely to get clot-busting drugs — and it isn't explained by age alone
studies.the_study: Using population-wide records for 59,346 adults hospitalized with ischemic stroke in Ontario between 2018 and 2022, researchers scored frailty from hospital data and examined who received thrombolysis (clot-dissolving drugs) or thrombectomy (mechanical clot removal). Nearly 39% of patients had high frailty scores. After adjustment, the most frail patients were about a third less likely than the least frail to receive thrombolysis (risk ratio 0.66 in women, 0.72 in men), yet frailty was not associated with lower thrombectomy rates. High frailty predicted higher 30-day mortality in men (RR 2.09) but not in women.
studies.why_it_matters: Frailty appears to be acting as an unspoken gatekeeper for one emergency stroke treatment but not another, which matters for the large share of older stroke patients who arrive at hospital already frail.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you or a partner has a stroke, frailty may influence what treatment is offered — but this study found no evidence that frailty consistently predicts worse outcomes in women. It is reasonable to ask the emergency team directly why a clot-busting drug is or isn't being offered, and whether the decision rests on the stroke itself or on general health status.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For hospitals and quality-measurement bodies, the finding argues that thrombolysis rates can't be compared across regions without adjusting for how frail the local stroke population is — and it raises the question of whether frailty is being applied as an informal exclusion criterion rather than an evidence-based one.
studies.caveats: Observational administrative-data study — cannot establish that frailty caused treatment decisions, and unmeasured factors such as stroke severity, pre-stroke function and patient or family preference were not fully captured. Frailty was derived from hospital coding rather than bedside assessment. Ontario-specific.

studies.title: Mild cognitive trouble often reverses — and a handful of everyday advantages predict who bounces back
studies.the_study: Researchers tracked 5,997 older Chinese adults across five waves of the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (2011-2020), producing 15,611 wave-to-wave transitions between four cognitive states. They scored each person on five resources: education beyond the lowest level, non-agricultural household registration, social participation, normal sleep duration, and absence of elevated depressive symptoms. Each additional resource was linked to substantially higher odds of moving back from impairment to unimpaired cognition (OR 1.40 from single-domain impairment, 1.32 from two-domain) and lower odds of progressing to impairment across multiple domains (OR 0.65 and 0.85).
studies.why_it_matters: It counters the assumption that cognitive decline only travels one direction: in this large cohort, people frequently returned to unimpaired status, and the factors tied to that recovery — sleep, mood, social involvement — are modifiable.
studies.story_angle_primary: If testing has flagged a weakness in one area of your thinking, that result is not necessarily permanent. Sleep duration, depressive symptoms and social participation were the three changeable items in this study's resource score, and all three are worth raising with your doctor as targets rather than accepting a single bad test as a verdict.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For senior living staff, the study supports treating depression screening, sleep hygiene and structured social programming as cognitive interventions, not just quality-of-life extras — and reframes residents with mild impairment as potentially improvable rather than simply on a downward track.
studies.caveats: Observational — cannot establish causation, and "apparent recovery" was based on repeated cognitive test scores, not clinically verified diagnoses, so measurement noise and practice effects may inflate recovery. The resource score mixes fixed social characteristics (education, household registration status) with modifiable behaviors. Chinese cohort; findings may not generalize elsewhere.

studies.title: An eye exam may flag which older adults' brains are silently aging fastest
studies.the_study: Researchers in Ecuador followed 241 older adults with prehypertension or hypertension who had retinal photographs and brain MRIs taken in 2013-2015, and re-scanned the 124 survivors who returned in 2025. Forty-one percent showed progression of white matter hyperintensities — the bright MRI spots that signal small vessel damage in the brain. Those who had moderate or worse hypertensive retinopathy (damage to the tiny blood vessels at the back of the eye) at the start were more than four times as likely to show that brain progression over the decade, even after accounting for age, blood pressure and other cardiovascular risk factors.
studies.why_it_matters: A routine, inexpensive retinal photograph may identify older adults whose brain's small blood vessels are deteriorating — damage linked to stroke risk, gait problems and cognitive decline — in places where repeated brain MRIs are unrealistic.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you have high or borderline blood pressure, the dilated eye exam you may already be getting for glaucoma or diabetes looks at the same kind of tiny vessels that supply your brain. It's worth asking your eye doctor whether they see signs of hypertensive damage, and making sure that finding gets back to the clinician managing your blood pressure — this study can't prove treating retinopathy protects the brain, but it suggests the eye is a useful window.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For care teams and senior living health coordinators: retinal findings are often siloed in optometry records and never reach primary care. This study is an argument for building the eye exam result into the resident's cardiovascular and cognitive risk picture rather than treating vision as a separate track.
studies.caveats: Observational design — cannot establish causation; only 51% of the original cohort completed follow-up imaging, and those lost had worse vascular burden at baseline; small number (17) with grade 2 or higher retinopathy; single rural Ecuadorian population that may not generalize.

studies.title: 'Hospital at home' looks very different depending on where you live — even inside one health system
studies.the_study: Investigators compared six of the VA's eleven Hospital in Home programs, which deliver hospital-level acute care in patients' own homes, using structured program presentations plus national VA administrative data. Core elements were consistent — interdisciplinary teams, formal clinical evaluation, informed consent, 24/7 access to the team — but almost everything else varied: the share of patients transferred from an inpatient bed ranged from 6% to 85%, nursing staffing from 4 to 7 full-time nurses, physician staffing from 1 to 2, and annual patient volume from 63 to 146. Referral pathways differed too, drawing variously on home-based primary care, outpatient clinics, specialty care and emergency departments.
studies.why_it_matters: Hospital-at-home is expanding rapidly as an alternative to inpatient admission for older adults, and this shows that two programs with the same name can operate very differently — so what a patient is offered depends heavily on the local program's design.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you or your spouse is offered 'hospital at home' instead of an inpatient admission, ask specific questions: Who comes to the house and how often? Is a physician involved daily? What happens at 2 a.m. if something goes wrong, and how fast can you be transferred back to the hospital? The answers legitimately differ from program to program, and you are entitled to know them before consenting.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For families and senior living operators coordinating with these programs: know which referral pathways your local program accepts — some take direct referrals from the emergency department or primary care, avoiding an inpatient stay entirely — and clarify in advance which ancillary services (therapy, labs, imaging, virtual follow-up) are bundled in.
studies.caveats: Descriptive study of only 6 of 11 VA programs, based partly on self-reported program presentations; no patient outcomes compared across sites; VA veteran population and VA infrastructure may not generalize to Medicare or private hospital-at-home programs.

studies.title: A cheap ratio from two routine blood tests tracks heart attack and stroke risk in diabetes
studies.the_study: Researchers at a single Chinese hospital reviewed records for 11,624 patients with type 2 diabetes, calculating a platelet-to-HDL-cholesterol ratio (PHR) from standard lab work already on file. Over a median 28.8 months, 18.8% had a major cardiovascular event — cardiovascular death, non-fatal heart attack or non-fatal stroke — and each standard-deviation increase in PHR was linked to a 20% higher risk in a roughly straight-line relationship. However, adding the ratio to existing risk models improved prediction only marginally (C-index 0.625 to 0.632).
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests that a risk signal for heart attack and stroke may already be sitting, unused, in blood work most people with diabetes get routinely — though the added predictive value here was small.
studies.story_angle_primary: You don't need to request a new test based on this study, but it's a reminder that the platelet count and HDL cholesterol already on your lab report carry cardiovascular meaning together, not just separately. At your next diabetes review, the more useful conversation is about the risk factors you can act on — blood pressure, HDL, smoking, activity — rather than any single new number.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For clinicians and care managers, this is a research-stage prognostic marker, not a tool for care planning; the honest message to families is that it does not yet change how cardiovascular risk is monitored in residents with diabetes.
studies.caveats: Single-center, retrospective and observational — cannot establish causation; participant age range not reported, so applicability to the oldest patients is unclear; improvement in prediction over standard models was very small; wide variation in follow-up time (IQR 5.0-67.5 months).

studies.title: A tape measure and a two-minute walk test can flag which heart failure patients are at highest risk
studies.the_study: Researchers analyzed 7,362 patients aged 65 and older hospitalized for heart failure in Japan's multicenter J-Proof HF Registry, splitting them chronologically into a training group (n=4,417) and a validation group (n=2,945). Using two simple bedside measures — calf circumference and the Short Physical Performance Battery (SPPB), a standard test of balance, walking speed and rising from a chair — they built a three-tier risk model. Patients with an SPPB of at least 10 and a calf circumference of 25.9 cm or more had the best one-year survival, while those with an SPPB under 7, or an SPPB of 7-9 with a calf under 25.3 cm, had the highest death rates; the pattern held in the validation cohort and in both sexes.
studies.why_it_matters: Two measurements that require nothing more than a tape measure, a chair and a stopwatch can identify which older heart failure patients most need nutrition support and rehabilitation — no imaging, blood work or specialist referral required.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you or a loved one is hospitalized for heart failure, it's reasonable to ask the care team whether anyone has measured your calf circumference and tested your walking speed, balance and ability to rise from a chair. These low-tech measures track muscle and nutrition status, and a poor result is a signal to ask about a referral for physical therapy and a dietitian assessment — not a verdict about your future.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For discharge planners and senior living clinical staff, this offers a practical triage tool that fits into a routine admission or move-in assessment: calf circumference plus SPPB takes minutes and can help prioritize which residents returning from a heart failure hospitalization get intensive rehab and nutrition follow-up first.
studies.caveats: Observational cohort — the model predicts risk but cannot establish that intervening on muscle mass or physical function changes outcomes. Conducted entirely in Japan, so the specific calf circumference cutoffs (25.3-25.9 cm) may not transfer directly to populations with different body sizes. Calf circumference can be inflated by fluid retention, a common problem in heart failure.

studies.title: A thicker brain in midlife doesn't guarantee sharper thinking after 80
studies.the_study: Investigators analyzed brain MRI scans and cognitive testing from cognitively healthy adults in the Human Connectome Project-Aging/Aging Adult Brain Connectome, spanning middle adulthood (36-59), early older adulthood (60-79) and late older adulthood (80+). They classified people as high, middle or low cognitive performers for their age and compared cortical thickness across the whole brain. The strongest links between a thicker cortex and better performance showed up for fluid abilities (problem-solving, processing speed) in midlife, concentrated in sensory and motor regions — and those differences faded with advancing age. Notably, the pattern was driven mostly by thinner cortex in low performers, not by any distinctive brain signature in high performers.
studies.why_it_matters: It challenges the assumption that brain structure seen on a scan explains who stays sharp into their 80s and 90s, suggesting that late-life cognitive strength depends on other mechanisms — a reason not to read too much into structural brain imaging as a predictor of your cognitive future.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you've ever worried about a scan showing brain 'thinning' or atrophy, this is context worth having: among cognitively healthy adults, the connection between cortical thickness and thinking ability got weaker with age, not stronger. Structural brain measures are only part of the picture, and in late life they explained relatively little about who performed well.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For clinicians and families interpreting imaging reports, the finding is a caution against over-reading structural changes in an older adult who is functioning well — cognitive performance in late life appears to rest on factors this kind of scan doesn't capture.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional design — this is a snapshot comparing different people at different ages, not the same people followed over time, so it cannot show how any individual's brain or cognition changes. Participants were cognitively healthy volunteers in a research cohort, who tend to be healthier and better educated than the general population. One senior author discloses a financial interest in a company (Niji Corp).

studies.title: A routine blood count may hold early clues about who develops Parkinson's disease
studies.the_study: Researchers analyzed 452 people with prodromal Parkinson's disease — early warning signs such as REM sleep behavior disorder or loss of smell, but no diagnosis — enrolled in the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative. They calculated five inflammation measures derived from an ordinary complete blood count and tracked who went on to develop diagnosable Parkinson's. Forty-three participants (9.5%) converted during follow-up, and one measure, the systemic inflammation response index, was independently associated with conversion (hazard ratio 2.34 per log-unit). Baseline inflammation levels — not changes over time — carried the predictive signal, and estimates were stronger in men.
studies.why_it_matters: If replicated, it suggests that a blood test already run in nearly every doctor's office might help gauge risk among people showing early Parkinson's warning signs, at essentially no added cost.
studies.story_angle_primary: This is early-stage research, not a test to request at your next appointment. But if you have known early warning signs of Parkinson's — such as acting out dreams, or a lost sense of smell — it's a reminder that research on inexpensive risk markers is moving quickly, and asking your neurologist about enrolling in a longitudinal study is one way to stay connected to it.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For care professionals, the practical near-term value is modest: the model's predictive accuracy was only fair (concordance statistic 0.683), so this does not yet change how anyone is counseled or monitored.
studies.caveats: Retrospective secondary analysis of an observational cohort — cannot establish that inflammation causes conversion. Only 43 conversion events, which the authors acknowledge limits precision; female estimates were too imprecise to interpret. No external validation in an independent cohort. PPMI participants are a selected research population and may not represent all older adults with early Parkinson's signs.

trends_raw:
**Convergent findings**

- **Structural and biological markers still describe where you are, not where you're going.** Last week's *Your "biological age" predicted how well you scored — but not how fast you declined* (PMID 42799693) is closely matched by this week's *A thicker brain in midlife doesn't guarantee sharper thinking after 80* (PMID 42784930), where the cortical thickness–cognition link faded with age and was driven by thinner cortex in low performers rather than any signature in high performers.
- **A label keeps acting as an informal exclusion criterion.** The prior digest's running theme of diagnosis-as-gatekeeper (frailty and cardiac rehab, dementia and heart attack care) gains a population-scale example in *Frail stroke patients are far less likely to get clot-busting drugs — and it isn't explained by age alone* (PMID 42803571), where frailty cut thrombolysis rates by about a third yet did not reduce thrombectomy rates or reliably predict worse outcomes in women.
- **Cheap, already-collected measures keep showing prognostic value.** *Vision loss doesn't just make life harder — it may move dementia up by two years* (PMID 42801054) is extended by *An eye exam may flag which older adults' brains are silently aging fastest* (PMID 42801966), and joined by *A tape measure and a two-minute walk test can flag which heart failure patients are at highest risk* (PMID 42800123) and *A routine blood count may hold early clues about who develops Parkinson's disease* (PMID 42778869).
- **Hope keeps outrunning the evidence in repurposed and new drugs.** Following *Adderall fails a 12-week test for cognitive problems in MS* (PMID 42800227), this week brings *Ambroxol for Parkinson's and Gaucher disease: the hype is running ahead of the evidence* (PMID 42801449) and *Across 1.2 million people, lithium users had about 37% less dementia — but no one has proven the drug is the reason* (PMID 42803710).
- **Movement and engagement hold their ground.** *Any activity beats none for quality of life in later years* (PMID 42800122) and *Having a sense of purpose keeps boredom at bay* (PMID 42773782) are reinforced by *Staying active still protects thinking skills in your 80s and 90s* (PMID 42803718), *Nine years of cycling later: these older athletes still outperform 99% of their peers* (PMID 42802250), and *Mild cognitive trouble often reverses* (PMID 42802990), whose modifiable ingredients were sleep, mood and social participation.

**Advances**

- **Anti-amyloid therapy moves from one clinic's experience to pooled numbers and real eligibility.** *Japan's first real-world look at lecanemab: 1 in 9 patients had brain imaging abnormalities* (PMID 42798750) is now flanked by *New Alzheimer's drugs slow decline — but a pooled analysis says the benefit may be too small for patients to notice* (PMID 42803728), which pools seven randomized trials and reports brain swelling in 23.9% of treated participants, and *Only about 1 in 9 memory clinic patients qualified for the new Alzheimer's drug* (PMID 42803707).
- **Biomarker caution becomes a diagnostic-accuracy problem.** Last week's *A blood test for Alzheimer's just cleared the FDA* (PMID 42800042) and *Not all Alzheimer's brain scans predict decline equally* (PMID 42787370) flagged that the test you get shapes the answer; PMID 42803707 shows the downstream consequence — clinical Alzheimer's diagnoses and amyloid results disagreed often, and 44% clinically diagnosed shrank to 26% amyloid-positive.
- **Program-level variation joins measurement-level variation.** Where the prior digest documented unreliable data systems, *'Hospital at home' looks very different depending on where you live — even inside one health system* (PMID 42802388) shows the same inconsistency in service delivery: within the VA, transfers from an inpatient bed ranged from 6% to 85% across six programs sharing one name.

**Counterpoints**

- **Decline is not always one-directional.** Most of the prior digest framed cognition as a downward trajectory to be predicted (PMIDs 42787370, 42799693); *Mild cognitive trouble often reverses — and a handful of everyday advantages predict who bounces back* (PMID 42802990) documents frequent returns to unimpaired status across 15,611 wave-to-wave transitions.
- **Aerobic fitness does not equal muscle preservation.** *Nine years of cycling later* (PMID 42802250) found lean tissue down 8.1% and body fat up even in dedicated endurance athletes — a caution against reading last week's general "any activity helps" message (PMID 42800122) as meaning any single type of activity suffices.

**New themes**

- **Hospital-level care delivered at home, and how much it varies by location:** PMID 42802388.
- **Discrimination-related stress as a treatable target, and technology older adults will actually use:** *Virtual reality "positive psychology" sessions eased stress for older Korean immigrants who faced discrimination* (PMID 42802583), with a mean participant age of 80.9.
- **Appetite as a barrier to strength training, tested and dismissed:** *Twelve weeks of strength training didn't change older men's appetite one way or the other* (PMID 42801941).
feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** Four studies published within days of each other put hard numbers on the distance between dementia-drug headlines and what happens in an actual clinic. *New Alzheimer's drugs slow decline — but a pooled analysis says the benefit may be too small for patients to notice* (PMID 42803728) found differences of well under half a point on cognitive scales alongside brain swelling in 23.9% of treated participants; *Only about 1 in 9 memory clinic patients qualified for the new Alzheimer's drug* (PMID 42803707) found just 11.7% of people with new memory complaints met the criteria for donanemab; and two reviews of cheaper hopes — *Across 1.2 million people, lithium users had about 37% less dementia* (PMID 42803710) and *Ambroxol for Parkinson's and Gaucher disease: the hype is running ahead of the evidence* (PMID 42801449) — describe encouraging signals that no trial has yet converted into proven benefit.

**Why pitch this now:** Families are walking into appointments having read that dementia is finally treatable, and this batch shows that most of them will not be eligible, that those who are face a modest benefit and real monitoring demands, and that the drugs being traded in online patient groups rest on thinner evidence still.

**Angle:** A calm, practical guide for older adults and adult children on how to evaluate a dementia or Parkinson's treatment claim — what "slows decline" actually measured, which questions confirm a diagnosis before treatment is discussed, and what to do when the answer is that you are not a candidate.

**Potential headlines:**
- In One Memory Clinic, Only 1 in 9 Patients Qualified for the New Alzheimer's Drug
- The Dementia Drugs Are Here, and Most People Who Want Them Can't Have Them
- What to Ask Before You Pin Your Hopes on a Dementia Treatment

**Potential outlets:**
- **Next Avenue** — its readers are often the adult child sitting in the neurology appointment, and this replaces vague optimism with the specific questions that decide eligibility.
- **Caring.com** — families at the decision stage need to know that a clinical Alzheimer's diagnosis is not the same as amyloid confirmation before they start shopping for an infusion center.
- **Being Patient** — a dementia-focused consumer publication that follows anti-amyloid treatment closely and has the audience most exposed to eligibility disappointment.
- **LeadingAge** — provider and memory-care members are the ones fielding these questions from residents' families and absorbing the transport and MRI monitoring burden.
pitch_ideas_raw:
- **Nine years of cycling later: these older athletes still outperform 99% of their peers (PMID 42802250):** Lifelong exercise didn't stop aerobic and muscle decline but kept these riders above the 90th percentile — with the twist that aerobic training alone didn't protect lean tissue, so strength work deserves equal billing, for a consumer aging-well feature and a senior-living wellness trade brief.
- **New Alzheimer's drugs slow decline — but the benefit may be too small for patients to notice (PMID 42803728):** Turn the pooled numbers into appointment questions — how much slowing to expect, what the MRI schedule involves, and whether APOE testing has been done, since ε4 carriers had roughly double the brain-swelling risk, for a consumer dementia explainer.
- **Across 1.2 million people, lithium users had about 37% less dementia (PMID 42803710):** A careful "curiosity, not a prescription" piece — why a promising old drug with kidney and thyroid risks still needs long-term trials, and why nobody should buy lithium supplements off a headline, for a consumer health explainer or a clinician-facing counseling brief.
- **Virtual reality "positive psychology" sessions eased stress for older Korean immigrants (PMID 42802583):** Participants averaging almost 81 years old used VR headsets willingly, and cultural and language tailoring is what made the program land — a programming lesson for senior centers serving immigrant elders, for a senior-living activities trade brief and a consumer piece on aging in immigrant families.
- **Ambroxol for Parkinson's and Gaucher disease: the hype is running ahead of the evidence (PMID 42801449):** The practical caregiver version — ask what off-label medications and supplements are actually in the pill organizer, and make sure the neurologist knows, for a caregiver-advice column or a Parkinson's patient publication.
- **Twelve weeks of strength training didn't change older men's appetite one way or the other (PMID 42801941):** Reassurance for anyone avoiding weights out of fear it will upset their eating — and a caution to dietitians that resistance work won't fix undereating either, for a consumer fitness explainer and a senior-living dining and rehab brief.
- **Staying active still protects thinking skills in your 80s and 90s (PMID 42803718):** The four-hour-a-week threshold works out to about 35 minutes a day of walking or gardening, and activity in this cohort collapsed from 64% to 16% after age 85 — a programming gap for the oldest residents, for a local-news health segment and a senior-living operations brief.
- **Only about 1 in 9 memory clinic patients qualified for the new Alzheimer's drug (PMID 42803707):** Ask what actually confirms the diagnosis, which eligibility criteria you meet, and what the plan is if you aren't a candidate — plus a concrete counseling number for staff, for a consumer dementia explainer and a memory-care clinical brief.
- **Frail stroke patients are far less likely to get clot-busting drugs (PMID 42803571):** It is fair to ask the emergency team whether a decision rests on the stroke itself or on general health status — and hospitals comparing thrombolysis rates need to adjust for local frailty, for a consumer health explainer and a hospital quality trade brief.
- **Mild cognitive trouble often reverses (PMID 42802990):** One weak test result is not a verdict — sleep, depressive symptoms and social participation were the changeable items linked to bouncing back, for a caregiver-advice column and a senior-living wellness brief that reframes mild impairment as potentially improvable.
- **An eye exam may flag which older adults' brains are silently aging fastest (PMID 42801966):** Ask your eye doctor whether they see hypertensive damage at the back of the eye, and make sure that result reaches whoever manages your blood pressure — retinal findings too often stay siloed in optometry records, for a consumer health explainer and a care-coordination trade brief.
- **'Hospital at home' looks very different depending on where you live (PMID 42802388):** A consent checklist for families offered hospital-level care at home — who comes to the house and how often, is a physician involved daily, what happens at 2 a.m., how fast can you transfer back, for a caregiver-advice column and a post-acute care trade brief.
- **A tape measure and a two-minute walk test can flag which heart failure patients are at highest risk (PMID 42800123):** Ask whether anyone measured calf circumference and tested walking, balance and rising from a chair after a heart failure hospitalization — and use it as a nudge toward rehab and a dietitian, for a consumer heart-health explainer and a discharge-planning trade brief.
- **A thicker brain in midlife doesn't guarantee sharper thinking after 80 (PMID 42784930):** Context for anyone rattled by a scan that mentions thinning or atrophy — in cognitively healthy adults the link between thickness and thinking got weaker with age, not stronger, for a consumer health explainer and a clinician-facing brief on interpreting imaging reports.
- **A routine blood count may hold early clues about who develops Parkinson's disease (PMID 42778869):** An honest early-research piece — not a test to request, but a reason for people with warning signs like acting out dreams or lost smell to ask about joining a longitudinal study, for a consumer neurology explainer.

fact_check.raw:
# Fact-Check Report: Senior Living Research Digest — New This Week — September 2026
**Checked:** 2026-09-28 | **Studies reviewed:** 16
**Primary audience:** older adults and seniors | **Secondary audience:** families, caregivers, and senior living professionals

---

### Study 1: Nine years of cycling later: these older athletes still outperform 99% of their peers — even as aging took its toll
**PMID:** 42802250 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Headline misreads percentile statistic** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "these older athletes still outperform 99% of their peers"
- **Abstract says:** "overall, 98.7% of those who completed the test were at or above the 90th percentile for V̇O2peak based on reference populations"
- **Problem:** 98.7% is the share of participants who reached the 90th percentile or better — not a percentile rank. The headline converts it into a claim that the cyclists outperform 99% of peers, which the data do not support (the study establishes top-10%, not top-1%, standing).
- **Suggested fix:** "Reword to something like: "nearly all of these older athletes still rank in the top 10% for aerobic fitness"."

**Issue B. Descriptor of participants not in abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "re-tested 82 of 125 lifelong recreational cyclists"
- **Abstract says:** "Of an original 125 cyclists first assessed in 2012-2013, 82 (53 males, 29 females) returned 9 years later"
- **Problem:** "Lifelong" and "recreational" are not stated in the abstract. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "Drop the adjectives or attribute them to the earlier cohort description."

**Issue C. Comparison to younger people not supported** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "staying active keeps you functioning at a level most people decades younger never reach"
- **Abstract says:** "98.7% of those who completed the test were at or above the 90th percentile for V̇O2peak based on reference populations"
- **Problem:** The abstract reports percentile standing against reference populations but says nothing about comparisons with people decades younger. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "Say they scored in the top 10% against reference populations, without the cross-generational comparison."

### Study 2: New Alzheimer's drugs slow decline — but a pooled analysis says the benefit may be too small for patients to notice
**PMID:** 42803728 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Pooled estimates presented as per-drug results** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "All three produced statistically significant but small improvements on cognitive and functional scales (CDR-SB difference of 0.41 points; MMSE 0.44 points)."
- **Abstract says:** "Seven trials were included. Treatment favored intervention for ADAS-Cog (SMD -0.15...), CDR-SB (MD -0.41...), and MMSE (MD 0.44...), although effects were small."
- **Problem:** The CDR-SB and MMSE figures are pooled across all seven trials, not drug-specific estimates; the abstract does not report separate per-drug effect sizes (though its conclusion does name all three drugs collectively).
- **Suggested fix:** "Write "Pooled across the trials, the antibodies produced statistically significant but small improvements (CDR-SB 0.41 points; MMSE 0.44 points).""

### Study 3: Across 1.2 million people, lithium users had about 37% less dementia — but no one has proven the drug is the reason
**PMID:** 42803710 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Headline pairs 1.2 million with the pooled hazard ratio** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Across 1.2 million people, lithium users had about 37% less dementia"
- **Abstract says:** "Twenty-three primary studies with original data (n > 1.2 million) were included in qualitative synthesis... Four cohort studies showed a pooled hazard ratio (HR) of 0.633 ... indicating ∼37% lower dementia risk with lithium."
- **Problem:** The 1.2 million figure covers the full qualitative synthesis; the 37% estimate is pooled from only four cohort studies. Pairing them in the headline overstates the base for the effect estimate.
- **Suggested fix:** ""Pooling four cohort studies, lithium users had about 37% less dementia" — with the 1.2 million total kept in the body."

**Issue B. Drinking-water framing not specified in abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "two ecological studies of water lithium levels pointed the same direction"
- **Abstract says:** "Two ecological studies using incidence rate ratios (IRR 0.830, 95% CI: 0.810-0.850) were directionally consistent."
- **Problem:** The abstract does not state that the ecological studies concerned lithium in drinking water. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "Say "two ecological studies" without specifying the exposure source, or attribute the detail to the full text."

### Study 4: Virtual reality "positive psychology" sessions eased stress for older Korean immigrants who faced discrimination
**PMID:** 42802583 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Attributing the effect to VR plus tailoring specifically** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "this is early evidence that immersive technology plus cultural tailoring — not one without the other — is what made the program land"
- **Abstract says:** "The results underscore the significance of advanced technologies with culturally tailored features to address mental health disparities and highlight the benefits of PPI."
- **Problem:** The two-arm trial compared the combined intervention against a wait-list; it did not dismantle the components, so it cannot show that either element was necessary.
- **Suggested fix:** "Say the program combined immersive technology with cultural tailoring, and that the trial could not separate the contribution of each."

**Issue B. Feasibility/uptake claims beyond abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "It is one of the first trials to show that adults in their 80s will readily use a VR headset"
- **Abstract says:** "Our study examines the feasibility and preliminary efficacy... We conducted descriptive statistics to assess the feasibility"
- **Problem:** The abstract reports that feasibility was assessed but gives no completion, adherence or acceptability figures, so "will readily use" and "older participants completed it" cannot be checked. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "Note that the authors assessed feasibility descriptively without citing specific uptake results."

### Study 5: Ambroxol for Parkinson's and Gaucher disease: the hype is running ahead of the evidence
**PMID:** 42801449 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 6: Twelve weeks of strength training didn't change older men's appetite one way or the other
**PMID:** 42801941 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 7: Staying active still protects thinking skills in your 80s and 90s, 30-year Jerusalem study finds
**PMID:** 42803718 | **Verdict:** ❌ Significant issues

**Issue A. Odds ratios assigned to wrong age intervals** — Severity: Major

- **As written:** "Being sedentary at age 78 roughly tripled the odds of cognitive impairment by 85 (OR 2.90), and being sedentary at 70 more than doubled the odds by 78 (OR 2.61)"
- **Abstract says:** "PA-S at baseline was found to have a statistically significant association with cognitive impairment at a later age between ages 78-85, 85-90: OR 2.61 (95%CI 1.38-4.82); OR 2.90 (95%CI 1.63-5.11), respectively."
- **Problem:** The abstract's OR 2.61 applies to the 78-to-85 interval and OR 2.90 to the 85-to-90 interval. The digest shifts both estimates one interval younger and reports a 70-to-78 finding the abstract never presents.
- **Suggested fix:** ""Being sedentary at 78 more than doubled the odds of cognitive impairment by 85 (OR 2.61), and being sedentary at 85 roughly tripled the odds by 90 (OR 2.90).""

**Issue B. Design described as a single followed cohort** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Researchers followed a community-dwelling cohort born in 1920-1921 in Jerusalem from 1990 to 2023, assessing participants at ages 70, 78, 85, 90, 95 and 100"
- **Abstract says:** "The Jerusalem Cross-sectional and Longitudinal Study (1990-2023) prospectively follows a representative community-dwelling cohort born 1920-1921, combining follow-up of the original cohort with repeated recruitment of same-birth cohort participants at each age."
- **Problem:** The design mixes longitudinal follow-up with fresh recruitment at each wave (which is why the n rises from 604 to 1,222), so the wave-by-wave activity percentages do not track the same people dropping out of exercise over time.
- **Suggested fix:** "Note that new same-birth-cohort participants were recruited at each assessment age, and that the activity-rate figures are cross-sectional snapshots."

### Study 8: Only about 1 in 9 memory clinic patients qualified for the new Alzheimer's drug
**PMID:** 42803707 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Reasons for ineligibility not reported** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "most people with memory complaints — including many diagnosed with Alzheimer's — do not qualify, often because they lack amyloid or have risk factors that make treatment unsafe"
- **Abstract says:** "Overall, 21 patients (11.7% of the total cohort and 45.6% of amyloid-positive individuals) fulfilled all AUR criteria for donanemab."
- **Problem:** The abstract gives eligibility proportions but does not break down which criteria patients failed, so the stated reasons are inference. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "State the eligibility proportions without specifying which criteria caused exclusion."

**Issue B. Diagnostic discordance stated at individual level** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "this study found that clinical Alzheimer's diagnoses and amyloid test results disagreed often"
- **Abstract says:** "A clinical diagnosis of AD was made in 78 (43.6%), and 46 (25.7%) were amyloid-positive."
- **Problem:** The abstract gives only aggregate counts and does not cross-tabulate clinical diagnosis against amyloid status, so patient-level disagreement rates are not reported.
- **Suggested fix:** "Say that clinical AD diagnoses (44%) outnumbered amyloid-positive results (26%) in this cohort."

### Study 9: Frail stroke patients are far less likely to get clot-busting drugs — and it isn't explained by age alone
**PMID:** 42803571 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Non-significant mortality result framed as no association** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "this study found no evidence that frailty consistently predicts worse outcomes in women"
- **Abstract says:** "High frailty was associated with an increased risk of 30-day mortality in males (2.09, 1.52-2.87), but not females (1.22, 0.90-1.66)."
- **Problem:** The female estimate is a point estimate of 1.22 with a confidence interval running up to 1.66 — imprecise rather than demonstrably null. Telling readers there is "no evidence" of worse outcomes overstates the certainty of a non-significant result.
- **Suggested fix:** ""In women, the link between frailty and 30-day death was not statistically significant, though the estimate still pointed upward.""

### Study 10: Mild cognitive trouble often reverses — and a handful of everyday advantages predict who bounces back
**PMID:** 42802990 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Intervention recommendation from observational data** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "the study supports treating depression screening, sleep hygiene and structured social programming as cognitive interventions, not just quality-of-life extras"
- **Abstract says:** "Resource advantage was associated with more favorable observed cognitive-domain transitions after localized impairment, but not clinically verified recovery."
- **Problem:** The study reports associations between a composite resource-count score and observed test-score transitions; it did not test any intervention, so it cannot support recommending these as cognitive interventions.
- **Suggested fix:** "Frame it as an association worth testing — e.g., "these modifiable factors travel with better cognitive trajectories and are plausible intervention targets for future trials.""

**Issue B. Frequency of recovery not quantified** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "in this large cohort, people frequently returned to unimpaired status"
- **Abstract says:** "Origin-state-restricted logistic models estimated apparent recovery from localized impairment and progression to multidomain impairment... 15,611 intervals from 5,997 respondents"
- **Problem:** The abstract reports odds ratios for apparent recovery but never gives the rate or share of participants who recovered, so "frequently" is not supported by reported figures.
- **Suggested fix:** "Say that recovery transitions occurred and were modeled, without characterizing how common they were."

**Issue C. Cognitive-state labels inferred** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "(OR 1.40 from single-domain impairment, 1.32 from two-domain)"
- **Abstract says:** "higher odds of S1-to-S0 apparent recovery (OR = 1.40...) and S2-to-S0 apparent recovery (OR = 1.32...)"
- **Problem:** The abstract labels the states only as S0-S3 and does not define what S1 and S2 represent, so the single-domain/two-domain gloss cannot be verified. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "Attribute the state definitions to the full text or describe them generically as lesser and greater degrees of localized impairment."

### Study 11: An eye exam may flag which older adults' brains are silently aging fastest
**PMID:** 42801966 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Cohort described as rural** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "single rural Ecuadorian population that may not generalize"
- **Abstract says:** "In this prospective study, 241 prehypertensive and hypertensive older adults underwent baseline clinical evaluations, retinal fundus photography, and brain MRI between 2013-2015. … a population-based cohort."
- **Problem:** The abstract describes a population-based Ecuadorian cohort but never says it is rural. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "Change to "single population-based Ecuadorian cohort that may not generalize.""

### Study 12: 'Hospital at home' looks very different depending on where you live — even inside one health system
**PMID:** 42802388 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 13: A cheap ratio from two routine blood tests tracks heart attack and stroke risk in diabetes
**PMID:** 42785601 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 14: A tape measure and a two-minute walk test can flag which heart failure patients are at highest risk
**PMID:** 42800123 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. SPPB called a "two-minute walk test"** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "A tape measure and a two-minute walk test can flag which heart failure patients are at highest risk"
- **Abstract says:** "The Short Physical Performance Battery (SPPB) is a validated predictor of adverse outcomes in HF."
- **Problem:** The SPPB is a three-part battery (balance, short gait-speed walk, chair rises), not a two-minute walk test — a distinct, differently named instrument. The digest body describes it correctly, so only the headline misleads.
- **Suggested fix:** "Reword the headline to "a tape measure and a short physical performance test" or "a brief balance-and-walking test.""

**Issue B. "Need" for treatment vs. need for assessment** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "can identify which older heart failure patients most need nutrition support and rehabilitation"
- **Abstract says:** "This bedside tool may help identify patients who could benefit from further nutritional and rehabilitation assessment."
- **Problem:** The abstract claims the tool flags candidates for further assessment; the digest upgrades this to identifying who needs the interventions themselves.
- **Suggested fix:** "Change to "which older heart failure patients most need further nutrition and rehabilitation assessment.""

### Study 15: A thicker brain in midlife doesn't guarantee sharper thinking after 80
**PMID:** 42784930 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Headline implies midlife-to-late-life tracking** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "A thicker brain in midlife doesn't guarantee sharper thinking after 80"
- **Abstract says:** "We analyzed cross-sectional data from cognitively healthy adults in the Human Connectome Project-Aging/Aging Adult Brain Connectome, spanning middle (36-59 years), early older (60-79), and late older (80 +) adulthood."
- **Problem:** The data are cross-sectional — different people at different ages — so nobody's midlife cortical thickness was followed to age 80. The headline reads as a within-person prediction, which the digest's own caveat says the study cannot support.
- **Suggested fix:** "Reword to something like "Cortical thickness tracks with thinking in midlife — but the link fades in the oldest adults.""

**Issue B. Extension to "90s"** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "It challenges the assumption that brain structure seen on a scan explains who stays sharp into their 80s and 90s"
- **Abstract says:** "spanning middle (36-59 years), early older (60-79), and late older (80 +) adulthood"
- **Problem:** The abstract defines the oldest group only as 80+, with no upper bound specified; the reference to the 90s goes slightly beyond what is stated.
- **Suggested fix:** "Say "into their 80s and beyond" or simply "in late life.""

### Study 16: A routine blood count may hold early clues about who develops Parkinson's disease
**PMID:** 42778869 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Sex difference reported without null interaction test** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Baseline inflammation levels — not changes over time — carried the predictive signal, and estimates were stronger in men."
- **Abstract says:** "Effect estimates were larger in male participants, while female estimates were imprecise as a result of limited events; no statistically significant biomarker-by-sex interaction was detected."
- **Problem:** The digest presents the male-female difference as a finding without noting the authors found no statistically significant interaction by sex, which makes the difference uninterpretable as a real effect modification.
- **Suggested fix:** "Add "though the difference between sexes was not statistically significant" after "stronger in men.""

**Issue B. Prodromal criteria not in abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "452 people with prodromal Parkinson's disease — early warning signs such as REM sleep behavior disorder or loss of smell, but no diagnosis"
- **Abstract says:** "We conducted a retrospective cohort analysis of 452 prodromal participants from the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative."
- **Problem:** The specific prodromal features (RBD, hyposmia) are plausible for PPMI but are not stated in the abstract. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "Attribute the examples to the PPMI enrollment criteria generally, or drop the specifics."

## Issue Summary

| Study # | Headline | Verdict | Notes |
|---------|----------|---------|-------|
| 1 | Nine years of cycling later: these older athletes still outperform 99% of their peers — even as aging took its toll | ⚠️ Minor issues | Body numbers match the abstract exactly, but the headline misreads the 98.7% figure as a percentile rank. |
| 2 | New Alzheimer's drugs slow decline — but a pooled analysis says the benefit may be too small for patients to notice | ⚠️ Minor issues | Effect sizes, ARIA rates and APOE stratification all match; only the per-drug attribution of pooled numbers is loose. |
| 3 | Across 1.2 million people, lithium users had about 37% less dementia — but no one has proven the drug is the reason | ⚠️ Minor issues | Numbers accurate; headline implies the 37% estimate came from all 1.2 million people when it came from four cohort studies. |
| 4 | Virtual reality "positive psychology" sessions eased stress for older Korean immigrants who faced discrimination | ⚠️ Minor issues | Sample, demographics and outcomes match; two inferences (component attribution and feasibility/uptake) go beyond the abstract. |
| 5 | Ambroxol for Parkinson's and Gaucher disease: the hype is running ahead of the evidence | ✅ Accurate | Screening counts, AMBITIOUS preprint status, heterogeneity and the author-involvement disclosure all match the abstract. |
| 6 | Twelve weeks of strength training didn't change older men's appetite one way or the other | ✅ Accurate | Sample, design, protocol, outcome measures and the null result are all reported faithfully, and the caveats cover the null-result and sample limitations. |
| 7 | Staying active still protects thinking skills in your 80s and 90s, 30-year Jerusalem study finds | ❌ Significant issues | The two odds ratios are attached to the wrong age intervals — the abstract reports 78-85 (OR 2.61) and 85-90 (OR 2.90), not 70-78 and 78-85. |
| 8 | Only about 1 in 9 memory clinic patients qualified for the new Alzheimer's drug | ⚠️ Minor issues | All eligibility percentages match; two small interpretive additions go slightly past the abstract. |
| 9 | Frail stroke patients are far less likely to get clot-busting drugs — and it isn't explained by age alone | ⚠️ Minor issues | Cohort size, frailty prevalence, risk ratios and the thrombolysis/thrombectomy contrast all match; one non-significant result is read as a null. |
| 10 | Mild cognitive trouble often reverses — and a handful of everyday advantages predict who bounces back | ⚠️ Minor issues | Sample, resource score and all four odds ratios match; the senior-living angle turns observational associations into service recommendations. |
| 11 | An eye exam may flag which older adults' brains are silently aging fastest | ⚠️ Minor issues | Numbers (241/124, 41% progression, HR 4.28, 17 with grade ≥2) all match; only the "rural" descriptor of the cohort is unsupported by the abstract. |
| 12 | 'Hospital at home' looks very different depending on where you live — even inside one health system | ✅ Accurate | All figures (6 of 11 programs, 6%-85% transfers, 4-7 FTE RNs, 1.0-2.0 FTE physicians, 63-146 patients/year, referral sources) match the abstract, and caveats correctly note the descriptive design and lack of outcome comparisons. |
| 13 | A cheap ratio from two routine blood tests tracks heart attack and stroke risk in diabetes | ✅ Accurate | N, median follow-up (28.8 months, IQR 5.0-67.5), 18.8% MACE, HR 1.20 per SD, and C-index 0.625→0.632 all match; framing is appropriately non-causal and avoids clinical recommendation. |
| 14 | A tape measure and a two-minute walk test can flag which heart failure patients are at highest risk | ⚠️ Minor issues | Sample sizes, cutoffs and risk-group definitions match the abstract; headline mislabels the SPPB and the "why it matters" slightly upgrades "assessment" to "support." |
| 15 | A thicker brain in midlife doesn't guarantee sharper thinking after 80 | ⚠️ Minor issues | Findings (fluid abilities in midlife, sensory/motor regions, effects driven by low performers, differences diminishing with age) and the Niji Corp disclosure are accurately reported; headline implies a longitudinal design the caveat correctly says does not exist. |
| 16 | A routine blood count may hold early clues about who develops Parkinson's disease | ⚠️ Minor issues | N=452, 43 (9.5%) phenoconversions, HR 2.34 per log-unit, c-statistic 0.683 and the baseline-vs-change finding all match; sex difference is stated without the abstract's caveat of no significant interaction, and the description of prodromal criteria isn't in the abstract. |

**Total issues:** 23 (18 Minor, 4 Moderate, 1 Major)
**Entries requiring revision:** 12
**Entries cleared:** 4
